learning_tracks.title: AI foundations: start from zero
learning_tracks.summary: Understand the vocabulary, what models can do, and where human judgment matters.

modules.title: AI, machine learning and generative AI
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is a broad name for computer systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence. Machine learning is one approach: a system learns patterns from data instead of having every rule written by hand.

Generative models produce new outputs such as text, images or audio based on patterns learned during training. An impressive answer is not proof of understanding or truth. The right first question is: what can I test?
modules.exercise: Write one example each of a rule-based program, a predictive model and a generative model. Explain how you would test each.

modules.title: How a language model writes
paragraphs: A language model generates sequences of tokens, which are pieces of text. It uses the context available to it to estimate what can follow. It does not automatically consult a trusted database of facts every time it answers.

Training, the information in your prompt, retrieval from external sources, and tools are different mechanisms. Ask whether an answer comes from the supplied source, a tool result or unsupported generation.
modules.exercise: Ask a model about an invented library function. Check the official documentation before trusting its answer.

modules.title: Your first useful prompt
paragraphs: Start with a task, relevant context, constraints and the output you need. A clear prompt reduces ambiguity but cannot guarantee correctness. Show a small example when the format matters.
Try a short task you already understand. Revise the instructions based on a specific failure rather than adding a long list of generic commands.
modules.exercise: Ask for an explanation of binary search. Add a concrete array and ask the model to walk through each iteration. Check it yourself.

modules.title: Check the answer before using it
paragraphs: Models can produce fluent errors, invented citations and insecure code. Verification should match the task: run tests for code, read cited sources for research, and recompute important numerical results.
When there is uncertainty, record it. For high-stakes decisions, use a qualified person and the relevant authoritative evidence. Do not treat model confidence as a reliability measure.
modules.exercise: Make a checklist for verifying a code answer, a factual answer and a research summary.

modules.title: Use AI responsibly as a student
paragraphs: Your institution and course determine what assistance is allowed. Keep records of assistance, acknowledge it when required, and make sure you can explain the final work.
Protect other people’s data. Do not upload personal information, unpublished research, credentials or private code unless you are authorized and understand how the provider handles it.
modules.exercise: Write your personal three-rule AI study policy. Include verification, attribution and privacy.

learning_tracks.title: Prompting that survives real work
learning_tracks.summary: Turn vague requests into repeatable tasks, examples and checks.

modules.title: Describe the job, not a magic phrase
paragraphs: A prompt is an instruction interface. Specify the task, the intended reader, relevant inputs and a useful output format. Avoid roleplay claims that promise expertise without evidence.
Work with small inputs so you can see what changed after each revision.
modules.exercise: Turn “help me study” into a prompt with a subject, time limit, question format and feedback rule.

modules.title: Use examples to define the format
paragraphs: Examples show what you mean more concretely than adjectives like “good” or “professional.” Include a representative input and the matching output.
Do not include real private records in examples. A synthetic example can define structure without exposing information.
modules.exercise: Create two examples for turning a meeting note into a task list. Include a note with no actionable task.

modules.title: Ground answers in supplied sources
paragraphs: Provide the evidence the task should use. Ask the model to separate statements supported by that evidence from unanswered questions.
A source reference only helps if it points to a real passage supporting the claim. Open and check the references.
modules.exercise: Provide a short article you may use. Ask for three claims with exact supporting passages, then verify each.

modules.title: Build a tiny evaluation set
paragraphs: Choose a small collection of examples before tuning the prompt. Include common inputs, ambiguous inputs and failure cases. Define success in a way another person could check.
A prompt that works on one example can still fail on the real task. Save prompt versions and compare them against the same examples.
modules.exercise: Write five test inputs for a study-question generator and a checklist for acceptable outputs.

learning_tracks.title: Code with AI and keep understanding
learning_tracks.summary: Use assistance for debugging and tests while owning your implementation.

modules.title: Read before you generate
paragraphs: Start with the repository README, entry points and existing tests. Ask for an explanation of a small part instead of an immediate rewrite.
You remain responsible for the result. Be able to explain every change you accept.
modules.exercise: Choose a small open repository. Trace one input from entry point to output.

modules.title: Write a failing example first
paragraphs: A reproducible example narrows debugging. State expected and actual behavior, input, environment and exact error. Ask for hypotheses before edits.
Use a regression test so a future change does not silently bring the bug back.
modules.exercise: Write a failing test for a function that mishandles an empty input, then fix the function.

modules.title: Review generated code
paragraphs: Check correctness, unsafe input handling, dependencies, licensing and secrets. Run the normal build and tests. A tool’s explanation is not independent verification.
Prefer small changes you can review. Separate generated suggestions from accepted code in your reasoning notes.
modules.exercise: Review a generated input parser with malformed, long and missing inputs.

modules.title: Document what you built
paragraphs: A good project README explains the problem, setup, usage, tests and known limitations. Include only results you actually observed.
A portfolio is stronger when you can discuss tradeoffs and failures, including where assistance was used.
modules.exercise: Write a five-section README for a small project and run its setup from a fresh folder.

learning_tracks.title: Your first reliable automation
learning_tracks.summary: Learn triggers, APIs, structured data, duplicate handling and safe retries.

modules.title: Triggers and actions
paragraphs: A workflow starts from a trigger, such as a schedule or webhook, and runs actions. Make the output of each step explicit.
Choose one source and one useful destination before building a complex chain.
modules.exercise: Draw a workflow that reads an RSS feed every day and stores article URLs.

modules.title: Read an API response
paragraphs: An API exposes a documented interface. Inspect status codes and JSON structure. Know which fields are required and which may be absent.
Use official APIs and authorized source pages. Keep credentials in the workflow credential store, not in code or output logs.
modules.exercise: Read a public JSON endpoint and list required, optional and unknown fields.

modules.title: Avoid duplicates and silent failures
paragraphs: Choose a stable identity, such as an original URL or source ID. An upsert updates an existing item instead of creating a duplicate on every run.
Retry transient failures with a bound. A failed fetch is not evidence that a source item has closed or disappeared.
modules.exercise: Run the same import twice. Confirm that the number of unique source URLs does not increase.

modules.title: Separate collection from publication
paragraphs: Collection produces candidates. Validation checks structure and source constraints. Review decides what should be public when important information is uncertain.
Keep the original link and collection time so a user can verify the record. Monitor source failures instead of hiding them.
modules.exercise: Design a pending-review state and identify three reasons to hold a collected item.

learning_tracks.title: From data to a first ML model
learning_tracks.summary: Build a baseline, split data correctly and evaluate what the model actually learned.

modules.title: Start with a question and a baseline
paragraphs: Define what you want to predict, what input is available at prediction time, and how the prediction will be used. Start with a simple baseline before using a complex model.
A useful metric depends on the task. Accuracy alone may be misleading for an imbalanced dataset.
modules.exercise: Choose an open dataset and write a baseline rule you can compare models against.

modules.title: Split before you learn from the data
paragraphs: Separate training data from validation and test data. Fit preprocessing on training data only. Leakage can make a model appear better than it is.
Time-dependent and grouped data often require a split that respects time or groups rather than random rows.
modules.exercise: Describe a leakage risk in a student-performance dataset and how to prevent it.

modules.title: Train a small model
paragraphs: Use a simple model with a reproducible random seed where relevant. Record features, preprocessing and parameter choices. Keep a final test set untouched while iterating.
Larger models are not automatically better for a small dataset or limited hardware.
modules.exercise: Train a baseline model and record validation results with the code needed to reproduce them.

modules.title: Inspect the mistakes
paragraphs: Look at the kinds of errors the model makes, not just a single metric. Check whether errors differ across important groups and inputs.
Document the dataset’s limits and avoid using a student experiment to make consequential decisions about people.
modules.exercise: Inspect ten wrong predictions and write an honest model limitations section.
